To make authentication visible and effortless on mobile without reinventing the wheel, stick to two dominant industry-standard mobile UX patterns:

1. Top-Right Header Icon (Simplest Integration)

On desktop, your user avatar sits on the far right. On mobile, users are already trained to look at the top-right corner for account settings.

Logged Out: Place a subtle user profile icon (👤) or a small text link ("Entrar") in the top right header, directly to the left of the hamburger menu (or replacing it entirely if redundant).

Logged In: Replace that icon with the circular profile picture avatar (matching desktop). Tapping it directly opens the profile view or a quick slide-down menu with "Mi Perfil" and "Cerrar sesión".

2. Bottom Navigation Tab Bar (Best for Mobile Engagement)

Bottom navigation bars comfortably hold 3 to 5 core destinations. Currently, your bottom bar has 5 items: Inicio, Agenda, Favoritos, +, and Noticias.

Why it works: Apps like Airbnb, Instagram, and Eventbrite use the bottom right slot for the profile. When logged out, tapping "Perfil" opens the login screen; when logged in, it lands on saved events, account settings, and published events.

3. Action-Triggered Contextual Auth (Bottom Sheet)

Don't rely solely on header/nav buttons to drive logins. Leverage intent-driven prompts:

When an unauthenticated user taps Favoritos (♥) or Publicar (+), slide up a native Mobile Bottom Sheet (half-screen modal): "Inicia sesión para guardar tus eventos favoritos" or "Inicia sesión para publicar".

This catches users right at the point of high intent, yielding significantly higher login conversion rates than passive top-level buttons.

Combining a persistent Top-Right Header Avatar with Contextual Bottom Sheets on your + and Favoritos buttons will give you the cleanest UX upgrade with minimal layout overhaul.

Yes to both, with one real wrinkle from what's actually in the code.

**Bottom-right over top-right.** Your own codebase already leans this way: `NavbarClient.tsx` swaps the Favoritos slot for a login icon when logged out (lines 245-266). You've half-built the bottom-tab pattern already. Formalizing it as a dedicated Perfil slot in position 5 is smaller than it sounds, and it fixes a real inconsistency: right now slot 3 changes *meaning* depending on auth state (Favoritos vs. Entrar), which is more confusing than having a stable Perfil slot that just changes its icon (outline person vs. avatar photo).

**Direct navigation, no dropdown.** Agreed, and for a concrete reason beyond taste: a 2-item dropdown (Ver perfil / Cerrar sessió) is an extra tap for the one thing people actually want, which is their profile. Instagram, Threads, and Airbnb all send the tab tap straight to the profile screen and bury logout inside it as a settings action. Your desktop dropdown at `NavbarClient.tsx:162-200` can stay as-is since space isn't scarce there, but mobile should drop it entirely.

One correction to the premise, though: the pasted analysis assumed profile is "duplicated" between top-right and bottom-right on your site today. It isn't. Right now mobile has zero avatar in the header, the only auth exposure is the hamburger's two-line menu plus that conditional Favoritos-slot icon. So this isn't a dedup job, it's a net-new bottom tab plus deleting the auth block from the hamburger panel (`NavbarClient.tsx:313-361`).

On Noticias, I'd push back a little on just deleting the tab. Before moving it into the Inicio feed, pull whatever click data you have on that nav item. If it's already low-traffic, moving it into a feed toggle is free. If it's not, you're trading a working channel for a hypothetical one on the strength of an Airbnb comparison, and Airbnb doesn't run an editorial section at all so the analogy is weaker there than for the profile question.

# PR Review Loop

Run AI code review to convergence on one PR, hands-off. One round = fetch → evaluate →
fix/decline → resolve → request re-review → wait. Loop rounds until diminishing returns.

This skill is **repo-agnostic**. The mechanics (gh GraphQL, bot triggers, the loop) are

## Round cap and termination

Stop the loop when ANY of these is true:
- A round produces **no new agreed fixes** (every new thread is a decline, or there are zero new unresolved threads).
- The new threads only **repeat already-declined** suggestions from a prior round.
- **5 rounds** have run (safety cap — report that the cap was hit, don't silently continue).

When stopping, report a final table: rounds run, fixed vs declined per round, and which condition ended the loop.

## Step 1 — Identify the PR

```bash
export GH_PAGER=cat
# Use the number if the user gave one; otherwise detect from the branch:
PR=$(gh pr view --json number --jq .number)
REPO=$(gh repo view --json owner,name --jq '"\(.owner.login)/\(.name)"')
```

If no PR exists for the branch, stop and tell the user to create one first (don't create it silently).

### Request Copilot's review (once, at the start)

Unlike the comment-triggered bots, GitHub Copilot is requested as a *reviewer* via the API. Do
it once when the loop starts (it then re-reviews on each push):

```bash
gh api --method POST "/repos/OWNER/REPO/pulls/PR_NUMBER/requested_reviewers" \
  -f "reviewers[]=copilot-pull-request-reviewer[bot]"
```

A `200` adds `Copilot` to the PR's requested reviewers and it reviews shortly after. A `422`
means Copilot code review isn't enabled for the repo/org (or the plan doesn't cover it) — note
it and carry on with the other bots, don't let it break the loop. Copilot posts inline review
comments, so Step 3 picks them up as threads with author `Copilot` and Step 4 evaluates them
like any other bot.

- The current repo's `CLAUDE.md` and `AGENTS.md` are usually already in context — use them.
- Look for a project review skill (e.g. `code-review-evaluation`) under `.github/skills/`, `.claude/skills/`, or `.agents/skills/`. If present, load it — it lists conventions external bots don't know (import rules, type organization, routing/searchParams restrictions, env-var rules, etc.).
- If the repo documents nothing relevant, fall back to generic review judgment (below).

The point: a suggestion that contradicts a documented project convention is a **decline with a reason**, not a fix.

## Step 3 — Fetch unresolved threads

```bash

gh api graphql -f query='
{
  repository(owner: "OWNER", name: "REPO") {
    pullRequest(number: PR_NUMBER) {
      reviewThreads(first: 50) {

          }
        }
      }
    }

}' --jq '.data.repository.pullRequest.reviewThreads.nodes[] | select(.isResolved == false) | {id, author: .comments.nodes[0].author.login, path: .comments.nodes[0].path, line: .comments.nodes[0].line, created: .comments.nodes[0].createdAt, body: .comments.nodes[0].body[0:300]}'
```

## Step 4 — Evaluate each suggestion

Default verdicts (override with project conventions from Step 2):

| Category | Default | Action |
|----------|---------|--------|
| Bug / error / edge-case fix (null check, try/catch, mkdir) | AGREE | Fix |
| Missing docs / fields | AGREE | Fix |
| Unused code / imports | AGREE | Fix |
| Extract constant / reduce duplication | AGREE | Fix |
| Performance (batch calls, avoid N+1) | AGREE | Fix |
| Security (generic patterns) | AGREE | Fix |
| Pattern / architecture change | CHECK PROJECT | Decide against repo conventions |
| Cosmetic refactor of working code | DECLINE | Resolve with rationale |
| Contradicts a documented project convention | DECLINE | Resolve, cite the convention |
| Repeat of a previously declined suggestion | DECLINE | Resolve, reference prior round |

Present a summary table before changing anything:

```
| # | Source | Line | Issue | Verdict |
|---|--------|------|-------|---------|
| 1 | Gemini L594 | Batch API calls | ✅ AGREE — N calls → 1 |
| 2 | Cubic L88   | Don't exit on error | ❌ DECLINE — CI needs to fail loud |
```

Read flagged sections (parallel reads), make minimal fixes, then validate with whatever the

One commit per round:

```bash

git commit -m "fix: address AI review feedback (round N)

- <fix 2> (Source)"
```

```bash

```

## Step 6 — Trigger the next review (only if needed)

The push in Step 5 already re-triggers most bots: CodeRabbit re-reviews incrementally on new
commits, and Gemini Code Assist usually re-syncs on push. **Check the repo's bot config — if

The bot posts a few minutes after the push. Don't busy-hold the session — schedule a single
re-check with `ScheduleWakeup` (~4 min) so the session is free meanwhile; one wake per round.

- New actionable threads → round N+1, back to Step 4.
- Nothing new after the wake → diminishing returns, stop.

let them re-invoke when the new review lands — same loop, user-paced.

3	description: Automate responding to AI code review comments (Gemini, CodeRabbit, Cubic, Sentry) on PRs. Use when asked to "check comments", "check new suggestions", or "respond to AI reviews".
4	---
5	
6	# AI Review Responder Skill
7	
8	## Purpose
9	
10	Automate the full cycle of responding to AI code review comments on GitHub PRs:
11	**Fetch → Evaluate → Fix/Decline → Resolve → Re-review**
12	
13	## When to Use
14	
15	Trigger phrases:
16	- "check comments", "check new suggestions", "check new comments"
17	- "respond to AI reviews", "handle review feedback"
18	- "check PR N for suggestions", "review PR comments"
19	
20	## Workflow
21	
22	### Step 1: Identify the PR
23	
24	- If the user specifies a PR number, use it
25	- Otherwise, detect from the current branch: `gh pr view --json number --jq .number`
26	- Get repo owner/name: `gh repo view --json owner,name --jq '"\(.owner.login)/\(.name)"'`
27	
28	### Step 2: Fetch Unresolved Threads
29	
30	**IMPORTANT**: Always set `export GH_PAGER=cat` before any `gh api` call to prevent pager issues.
31	
32	```bash
33	export GH_PAGER=cat
34	gh api graphql -f query='
35	{
36	  repository(owner: "OWNER", name: "REPO") {
37	    pullRequest(number: PR_NUMBER) {
38	      reviewThreads(first: 50) {
39	        nodes {
40	          id
41	          isResolved
42	          comments(first: 1) {
43	            nodes {
44	              createdAt
45	              author { login }
46	              path
47	              line
48	              body
49	            }
50	          }
51	        }
52	      }
53	    }
54	  }
55	}' --jq '.data.repository.pullRequest.reviewThreads.nodes[] | select(.isResolved == false) | {id: .id, author: .comments.nodes[0].author.login, path: .comments.nodes[0].path, line: .comments.nodes[0].line, created: .comments.nodes[0].createdAt, body: .comments.nodes[0].body[0:300]}'
56	```
57	
58	If no unresolved threads, report "No new comments" and stop.
59	
60	### Step 3: Evaluate Each Suggestion
61	
62	For each unresolved thread, use the `code-review-evaluation` skill's decision tree:
63	
64	| Category | Default | Action |
65	|----------|---------|--------|
66	| Bug/error fix | AGREE ✅ | Fix it |
67	| Missing docs/fields | AGREE ✅ | Fix it |
68	| Unused code/imports | AGREE ✅ | Fix it |
69	| Extract constant / reduce duplication | AGREE ✅ | Fix it |
70	| Edge case handling (null check, mkdir, try/catch) | AGREE ✅ | Fix it |
71	| Performance improvement (batch API calls) | AGREE ✅ | Fix it |
72	| Pattern/architecture change | CHECK SKILLS | Cross-reference project skills |
73	| Cosmetic refactor (rename, reorder working code) | DECLINE ❌ | Resolve with rationale |
74	| Repeat of previously declined suggestion | DECLINE ❌ | Resolve, reference prior decision |
75	| Breaks functionality or project conventions | DECLINE ❌ | Resolve with explanation |
76	
77	**For pattern/architecture suggestions**: Cross-reference the relevant project skill from `.github/skills/` before deciding. See the `code-review-evaluation` skill for the full decision tree.
78	
79	### Step 4: Present Summary Table
80	
81	Before making changes, present a summary table:
82	
83	```
84	| # | Source | Line | Issue | Verdict |
85	|---|--------|------|-------|---------|
86	| 1 | Gemini L594 | Batch API calls | ✅ AGREE — reduces N calls to 1 |
87	| 2 | Cubic L88 | Don't exit on error | ❌ DECLINE — rationale here |
88	```
89	
90	### Step 5: Apply Fixes
91	
92	For agreed suggestions:
93	1. Read the relevant code sections (parallel reads for efficiency)
94	2. Make the minimal fix
95	3. Validate (syntax check, lint, typecheck as appropriate for the language)
96	
97	Batch all fixes into a single commit:
98	
99	```bash
100	git add <files>
101	git commit -m "fix: address AI review feedback (round N)
102	
103	- [description of fix 1] (Source)
104	- [description of fix 2] (Source)
105	
106	Co-authored-by: Copilot <223556219+Copilot@users.noreply.github.com>"
107	```
108	
109	If push is rejected (non-fast-forward), use `git pull --rebase && git push`.
110	
111	### Step 6: Resolve All Threads
112	
113	Resolve ALL threads (both fixed and declined) using GraphQL mutation:
114	
115	```bash
116	for TID in "THREAD_ID_1" "THREAD_ID_2"; do
117	  gh api graphql \
118	    -F tid="$TID" \
119	    -f query='mutation($tid: ID!) {
120	      resolveReviewThread(input: {threadId: $tid}) {
121	        thread { isResolved }
122	      }
123	    }' --jq '.data.resolveReviewThread.thread.isResolved'
124	done
125	```
126	
127	### Step 7: Request Re-review
128	
129	Post a summary comment and trigger review bots:
130	
131	```bash
132	cat <<'EOF' > /tmp/review-comment.md
133	Round N: [summary of fixes]. Declined: [summary with rationale].
134	
135	@coderabbitai review
136	@gemini review
137	@cubic-dev-ai review
138	EOF
139	gh pr comment PR_NUMBER --body-file /tmp/review-comment.md
140	```
141	
142	**Bot trigger commands**:
143	- CodeRabbit: `@coderabbitai review`
144	- Gemini: `@gemini review`
145	- Cubic: `@cubic-dev-ai review`
146	
147	### Step 8: Report Results
148	
149	Present a final summary table showing all actions taken.
150	
151	## Evaluation Rules
152	
153	### Always Agree (Most Cases)
154	
155	AI reviewers are usually right about:
156	- Missing null checks, error handling, edge cases
157	- Unused imports/variables
158	- Documentation inconsistencies
159	- Type mismatches
160	- Extracting repeated values as constants
161	- Reducing API call count (batching)
162	- File encoding, trailing newlines
163	- Security vulnerabilities (generic patterns)
164	
165	### Check Project Skills Before Deciding
166	
167	Only when suggestion involves project-specific patterns. See `code-review-evaluation` skill for full list:
168	- Import patterns (`next/link` vs `@i18n/routing`)
169	- Type organization (`/types` directory governance)
170	- Styling (semantic tokens vs arbitrary Tailwind)
171	- API patterns (three-layer proxy, `fetchWithHmac`)
172	- URL/routing (`searchParams` restrictions)
173	- Environment variables (4-location rule)
174	
175	### Common Decline Patterns
176	
177	| Pattern | Typical Rationale |
178	|---------|------------------|
179	| Cosmetic refactor of working code | Adds risk without functional benefit |
180	| Consolidate queries with different filters | Different queries need different parameters |
181	| Replace string ops with stdlib for controlled inputs | Input is a constant we control |
182	| Split small scripts into modules | Acceptable for scripts under ~1500 lines |
183	| Don't exit on missing required config in CI | CI scripts can't produce useful output without config |
184	| Broader exception handling | Specific catches are intentional |
185	| Repeated suggestion (same as prior round) | Already evaluated and declined with rationale |
186	
187	## Efficiency Tips
188	
189	- **Parallel reads**: Read all flagged code sections in one tool call
190	- **Batch edits**: Apply all fixes before committing
191	- **Single commit**: Group all fixes into one commit per round
192	- **Single resolve loop**: Resolve all thread IDs in one bash call
193	- **Count rounds**: Track which round this is (check PR comment history)
194	- **Handle push conflicts**: Always `git pull --rebase` if push fails
195	
196	## Example Full Run
197	
198	```
199	User: "check new comments"
200	
201	Agent:
202	1. Detects PR from current branch
203	2. Fetches 4 unresolved threads
204	3. Presents table:
205	   | # | Source | Issue | Verdict |
206	   |---|--------|-------|---------|
207	   | 1 | Cubic L200 | Add mkdir before write | ✅ Fix |
208	   | 2 | Cubic L50 | Don't exit on error | ❌ Decline — can't run without config |
209	   | 3 | Gemini L100 | Consolidate queries | ❌ Decline — different filters |
210	   | 4 | Gemini L300 | Use urlparse | ❌ Decline — input is constant |
211	
212	4. Fixes #1, validates syntax
213	5. Commits and pushes
214	6. Resolves all 4 threads
215	7. Posts summary comment + triggers re-review bots
216	8. Reports: "Round N: 1 fixed, 3 declined. All resolved."
217	```
218	
219	## Checklist
220	
221	- [ ] Set `export GH_PAGER=cat` before GraphQL calls
222	- [ ] Fetch ALL unresolved threads (not just new ones)
223	- [ ] Cross-reference `code-review-evaluation` skill for pattern/architecture suggestions
224	- [ ] Present summary table before making changes
225	- [ ] Validate changes after fixes (syntax, lint, typecheck)
226	- [ ] Handle `git push` rejection with `--rebase`
227	- [ ] Resolve ALL threads (fixed AND declined)
228	- [ ] Include round number in commit and comment
229	- [ ] Trigger review bots using correct commands (`@gemini review`, not `/gemini review`)

5	
6	# Code Review Evaluation Skill
7	
8	## Purpose
9	
10	Evaluate external code review suggestions (Gemini, CodeRabbit, etc.) against project conventions. These tools have access to our codebase and often make valid suggestions - but they don't know our **project-specific conventions**.
11	
12	## What External Reviewers ARE Good At
13	
14	CodeRabbit, Gemini, etc. **can see your code** and are excellent at catching:
15	
16	- ✅ **Missing fields** in examples/docs (like missing `geoScope` in docstring)
17	- ✅ **Type mismatches** and inconsistencies
18	- ✅ **Unused imports/variables**
19	- ✅ **Potential null/undefined errors**
20	- ✅ **Security vulnerabilities** (generic patterns)
21	- ✅ **Documentation gaps**
22	- ✅ **Test coverage suggestions**
23	- ✅ **General best practices** (accessibility, performance)
24	
25	**These suggestions are usually VALID - agree with them!**
26	
27	## What External Reviewers DON'T Know
28	
29	They lack context about our **project-specific conventions**:
30	
31	- ❌ Our `@i18n/routing` Link requirement
32	- ❌ Our `/types` directory governance
33	- ❌ Our three-layer API proxy pattern
34	- ❌ Our design system semantic classes
35	- ❌ Our env variable 4-location rule
36	- ❌ Our $300 searchParams incident history
37	
38	**Only check skills when suggestion involves these patterns.**
39	
40	## Evaluation Framework
41	
42	When user asks "Do you agree with this suggestion?":
43	
44	### Step 1: Categorize the Suggestion
45	
46	| Category            | Examples                                   | Default Response  |
47	| ------------------- | ------------------------------------------ | ----------------- |
48	| **Bug/Error fix**   | Missing field, type error, null check      | Usually **AGREE** |
49	| **Documentation**   | Missing JSDoc, outdated example            | Usually **AGREE** |
50	| **Code quality**    | Unused code, simplification                | Usually **AGREE** |
51	| **Code complexity** | >100 lines/function, >10 props, >3 nesting | Usually **AGREE** |
52	| **Pattern change**  | Different import, new abstraction          | **CHECK SKILLS**  |
53	| **Architecture**    | Component structure, API calls             | **CHECK SKILLS**  |
54	
55	### Step 2: If Pattern/Architecture → Cross-Reference Skills
56	
57	Only check skills if the suggestion involves patterns we have rules for:
58	
59	| Skill                          | Check For                                           |
60	| ------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------- |
61	| `pre-implementation-checklist` | Does suggestion duplicate existing code?            |
62	| `type-system-governance`       | Does it create types outside `/types`?              |
63	| `react-nextjs-patterns`        | Does it violate server-first pattern?               |
64	| `api-layer-patterns`           | Does it bypass three-layer proxy?                   |
65	| `url-canonicalization`         | Does it add `searchParams` to listing pages?        |
66	| `i18n-best-practices`          | Does it use `next/link` instead of `@i18n/routing`? |
67	| `design-system-conventions`    | Does it use `gray-*` or arbitrary utilities?        |
68	| `env-variable-management`      | Does it add env var without all 5 locations?        |
69	| `data-validation-patterns`     | Does it skip Zod validation?                        |
70	| `security-headers-csp`         | Does it use raw `fetch()` without wrappers?         |
71	
72	### Step 3: Provide Structured Response
73	
74	## Response Template
75	
76	```markdown
77	## Evaluation: [Suggestion Title/Topic]
78	
79	### Summary
80	
81	[1-2 sentence summary of the suggestion]
82	
83	### Category
84	
85	[Bug fix / Documentation / Code quality / Pattern change / Architecture]
86	
87	### Skill Check (if pattern/architecture)
88	
89	- [ ] [Relevant skill] - [Pass/Conflict: reason]
90	
91	### Recommendation
92	
93	**[AGREE / DISAGREE / PARTIAL]**
94	
95	[Explanation]
96	```
97	
98	## Example: Valid Suggestion (AGREE)
99	
100	**CodeRabbit says**: "Docstring example missing geoScope field"
101	
102	```markdown
103	## Evaluation: Missing geoScope in docstring
104	
105	### Summary
106	
107	Example in JSDoc is missing a required field from the type.
108	
109	### Category
110	
111	Documentation - external reviewer caught a real inconsistency.
112	
113	### Skill Check
114	
115	Not needed - this is a documentation fix, not a pattern change.
116	
117	### Recommendation
118	
119	**AGREE** - The docstring example should match the actual type definition.
120	```
121	
122	## Project-Specific Blind Spots (CHECK SKILLS)
123	
124	Only disagree when suggestion conflicts with our conventions:
125	
126	### 1. "Use `next/link` directly"
127	
128	**Our rule**: Always use `Link` from `@i18n/routing`
129	**Response**: Disagree - breaks locale handling
130	
131	### 2. "Add types inline in component"
132	
133	**Our rule**: All types in `/types` directory
134	**Response**: Disagree - violates type governance
135	
136	### 3. "Use `gray-500` for text"
137	
138	**Our rule**: Use semantic tokens (`text-foreground/80`)
139	**Response**: Disagree - violates design system
140	
141	### 4. "Add searchParams to page component for filtering"
142	
143	**Our rule**: NEVER in listing pages (causes $300+ cost spikes)
144	**Response**: Disagree - violates url-canonicalization (CRITICAL)
145	
146	### 5. "Use raw fetch() for this API call"
147	
148	**Our rule**: Use `fetchWithHmac` or `safeFetch`
149	**Response**: Disagree - violates security patterns
150	
151	### 6. "Create a helper function here"
152	
153	**Our rule**: Search for existing patterns first
154	**Response**: Partial - check if pattern exists before creating
155	
156	### 7. "Use axios instead of fetch"
157	
158	**Our rule**: Use `fetchWithHmac` (internal) or `safeFetch` (external)
159	**Response**: Disagree - we have standardized fetch wrappers
160	
161	### 8. "Prefer @types/\* path alias over bare types/ path"
162	
163	**Our rule**: Use `types/*` not `@types/*`
164	**Response**: Disagree - `@types/*` conflicts with TypeScript's convention for type definition packages (e.g., `@types/react`, `@types/node`). We intentionally use `types/*` to avoid this collision.
165	
166	## Quick Decision Tree
167	
168	```text
169	Is the suggestion about...?
170	│
171	├─ Bug/error fix → Usually AGREE ✅
172	├─ Missing docs/fields → Usually AGREE ✅
173	├─ Unused code cleanup → Usually AGREE ✅
174	├─ Test coverage → Usually AGREE ✅
175	│
176	├─ Types/interfaces → Check type-system-governance
177	├─ Components → Check react-nextjs-patterns
178	├─ Styling → Check design-system-conventions
179	├─ API calls → Check api-layer-patterns
180	├─ URLs/routing → Check url-canonicalization
181	├─ Links → Check i18n-best-practices
182	├─ Env vars → Check env-variable-management
183	├─ Validation → Check data-validation-patterns
184	├─ Security → Check security-headers-csp
185	├─ New utility → Check pre-implementation-checklist
186	```
187	
188	## More Examples
189	
190	### Example: Missing Field in Docstring (AGREE)
191	
192	**Suggestion**: "Docstring example missing geoScope field"
193	
194	**Response**: **AGREE** - External reviewer correctly identified inconsistency between example and type.
195	
196	### Example: Suggestion to use `useMemo` (PARTIAL)
197	
198	**Suggestion**: "Wrap this computation in useMemo for performance"
199	
200	**Response**: **PARTIAL** - Only if profiling shows actual bottleneck. Don't prematurely optimize.
201	
202	### Example: Suggestion to inline styles (DISAGREE)
203	
204	**Suggestion**: "Use inline className with Tailwind utilities"
205	
206	**Response**: **DISAGREE** - `design-system-conventions` requires semantic classes.
207	
208	## When to AGREE (Most Cases)
209	
210	External reviewers are usually right about:
211	
212	- Missing fields in docs/examples
213	- Type inconsistencies
214	- Unused imports/variables
215	- Null/undefined safety
216	- Documentation improvements
217	- Test coverage gaps
218	- Accessibility issues
219	- General security issues
220	
221	## When to DISAGREE (Project-Specific)
222	
223	Only disagree when suggestion conflicts with our skills:
224	
225	- Uses `next/link` instead of `@i18n/routing`
226	- Creates types outside `/types`
227	- Uses `gray-*` instead of semantic tokens
228	- Adds `searchParams` to listing pages
229	- Uses raw `fetch()` instead of our wrappers
230	- Bypasses three-layer API pattern
231	- Adds env var without 4-location update
232	
233	## Checklist
234	
235	- [ ] What category is this? (Bug fix / Docs / Code quality / Pattern)
236	- [ ] If pattern change → check relevant skills
237	- [ ] Does it conflict with project conventions?
238	- [ ] Provide clear AGREE / DISAGREE / PARTIAL response

Confirmed the mechanism (checked `lib/auth/enrichment.ts:83-92`): Logto's `username` claim can carry an email, and enrichment only overrides it with a backend value when that backend value isn't itself email-shaped — otherwise it falls back to the original, so an email-shaped `username` genuinely can survive a "successful" enrichment. Cubic's technical claim is accurate.

But the fix cubic implies — loosening `usernameLocked` (`EditProfileForm.tsx:36`) — touches a documented, deliberate one-time-lock invariant ("usernames feed indexed public URLs, so the backend only allows setting a real one once"). That's worth its own scoped PR with its own tests, not a bolt-on inside a mobile-nav rework. And critically: this isn't a regression from this PR. Before this PR, a user in this exact state had *no* profile link at all on mobile (the old hamburger only rendered `{profileHref && ...}`) — strictly worse than now, where they at least reach a page with a working logout button.
